## MultiZenoTravel problems {#sec-model}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Instances, plans, Pareto fronts, assumptions and patterns
:::

In this Section, we introduce three versions of the MultiZenoTravel problem: the symmetric clique
MultiZenoTravel, the non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel and the general MultiZenoTravel. We then
make precise what a plan is, together with its cost and its makespan, and the assumptions on
durations used in the rest of the paper. Plans are defined flight by flight, with explicit
departure times, so that waiting, passengers changing planes, empty flights and flights between
central cities are part of the problem and not excluded by assumption. The characterization of the
Pareto-optimal plans comes next: for the [symmetric clique problem](#sec-front) first, then for the
[non-symmetric and general problems](#sec-nonsymmetric).

### Instances {#sec-instances}

Let us introduce some notations related to the planning problem briefly presented in the
introduction: a non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel instance
([schematic view](#fig-instance)) is defined by the following elements
({{< node "Definition 1.1" >}}):

* $n$ central cities, organized as a clique in which every node is connected to $C_I$ and $C_G$,
  respectively the initial city and the goal city.
* $c \in \mathbb N^n$, where $c_i$ is the cost for landing in $C_i$.
* $D \in \mathbb N^{n \times n}$, where $d_{ij}$ is the flying time from $C_i$ to $C_j$.
* $d \in \mathbb N^n$, where $d_i$ is the flying time between $C_I$ and $C_i$.
* $\bar d \in \mathbb N^n$, where $\bar d_i$ is the flying time between $C_i$ and $C_G$.
* $p$ planes, initially in $C_I$, that have a capacity of a unique person.
* $t$ persons, initially in $C_I$.

The goal of MultiZenoTravel is to carry all $t$ persons, initially in $C_I$, to $C_G$ using $p$
planes, minimizing both the makespan and the cost of the plan.

A flight between a hub and a central city takes the same time in both directions, and there is no
flight between $C_I$ and $C_G$. The table $D$ is complete and directed: for every ordered pair
$(i, j)$ of central cities, $i = j$ included, the flight from $C_i$ to $C_j$ lasts $d_{ij}$; the
results that need a condition on these flights state it ([assumptions](#sec-assumptions)). We
write $\mathrm{dur}(a, b)$ for the duration of the flight from $a$ to $b$. Landing in $C_I$ or
$C_G$ is free. Finally, we only consider cases where $t \ge p$.

An instance of the symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel problem is an instance such that
$d = \bar d$. A general MultiZenoTravel instance is an instance such that the $n$ central cities
are organized as an arbitrary graph; it is defined in the
[general section](#sec-graphs).

Throughout the paper, we illustrate the definitions on the symmetric instance with $n = 3$
cities, $t = 3$ passengers and $p = 2$ planes, durations $d = (2, 3, 5)$ and costs
$c = (9, 6, 1)$ (the file
[`site/problem/example.dat`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/site/problem/example.dat),
also used on the [Problem](../problem.qmd) page). Its Pareto front, as (cost, makespan), computed
by ZenoSolver and by the verified solver of the [Verification](#sec-verification) section, is
$$(4, 20),\ (14, 16),\ (20, 14),\ (24, 12),\ (30, 10),\ (36, 8)$$
for every table of flights between central cities: the certificate ZenoSolver writes for it closes
every gap with the relaxation of the [next section](#sec-relaxation).

::: {#fig-plan .plan-display}

$$
\begin{array}{lllllll}
p_1: & C_I & \overset{t_1}{\to} C_2 & \to C_I & \overset{t_2}{\to} C_3 & \overset{t_2}{\to} C_G & \\
p_2: & C_I & \overset{t_3}{\to} C_3 & \overset{t_3}{\to} C_G & \to C_2 & \overset{t_1}{\to} C_G &
\end{array}
$$

Example of an admissible plan to transport 3 travelers via 2 planes, on the instance above. This
representation indicates the successive actions for each plane. We noted by
$\overset{t_i}{\to}$ a flight with a traveler.
:::

@fig-plan illustrates an admissible solution, of cost 14 and makespan 16. Note that the makespan
for a plan is not necessarily the largest sum of the flights' duration as some planes might have
to wait for others. This would be the case for $p_2$ waiting for $t_1$ in $C_2$, had it reached
$C_2$ before $p_1$ dropped $t_1$ there.

### Plans {#sec-plans}

To reason about all plans, including those that wait, hand passengers over or fly between
central cities, we fix their semantics ({{< node "Definition 1.2" >}}). A *leg* is a flight of
one plane, from its origin to its destination, with a departure time in $\mathbb N$, an arrival
time equal to the departure plus the duration of the flight, and at most one passenger on board.
A list of legs is a *route from $x$ at time $\tau$* if its first leg leaves $x$ no earlier than
$\tau$ and each later leg leaves where the previous one arrived, no earlier than that arrival. A
plan gives each plane a list of legs, and it is *feasible* if

1. the legs of each plane form a route from $C_I$ at time 0 whose last leg arrives in $C_G$;
2. for every passenger, the legs that carry it, its *journey*, form, in some order, a route from
   $C_I$ at time 0 whose last leg arrives in $C_G$.

A leg names at most one passenger, which is the capacity constraint. The *cost* $C$ of a plan is
the sum of the landing costs of all its legs that land in a central city, with or without a
passenger, and its *makespan* $M$ is the time at which the last plane reaches $C_G$ for the last
time, the arrival of the last leg of a route. $\mathcal A$ is the set of pairs $(C, M)$ of
feasible plans. The *flight time* $F_k$ of plane $k$ is the sum of the durations of its legs; its
flights are sequential, so $F_k \le M$.

Waiting is implicit: a plane or a passenger may depart later than it arrived. Boarding and
deplaning take no time, several planes may be in a city at once, and a passenger may change
planes in any city, any number of times. In @fig-plan, $t_1$ changes planes once, in $C_2$.
Times are natural numbers: a plan with rational or real times and the same integer durations,
rounded down, becomes a feasible plan with the same cost and a makespan no larger
({{< node "Lemma 1.3" >}}).

Requiring planes to finish in $C_G$ does not change the front: if planes may end anywhere, the
legs of a plane forming a route from $C_I$ at time 0, possibly empty, and the makespan being the
last arrival of any leg, the Pareto front is the same under the assumptions of the next section
({{< node "Theorem 4.5" >}}). All the planes may thus be assumed to finish their respective
sequence in $C_G$.

Journeys may contain detours that serve nothing; what a passenger needs of its journey is a
chain:

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 3.2" >}} **Chains.** *(a)* In a feasible plan, and in a plan whose planes end
anywhere, every passenger rides a *chain*: legs of the plan that carry it, the first leaving
$C_I$, each later one leaving where the previous one arrived and no earlier, all landing in central
cities except the last, which arrives in $C_G$. *(b)* If the plan has no flight between central
cities, every passenger rides a leg $C_I \to C_x$ and then a leg $C_x \to C_G$ that leaves no
earlier than the first one arrives.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Keep the part of the journey from its last departure from $C_I$ to the first later
arrival in $C_G$; none of its legs arrives in $C_I$
({{< node "Lemma 3.2" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

ZenoSolver outputs each instance as a PDDL file[^pddl] for the domain
[`pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl):
a durative `fly` action that adds the landing cost to `total-cost`, instantaneous `board` and
`debark` actions, and a predicate `libre` that enforces capacity one. The plans above abstract
this domain: the `fly` actions of a plane are its legs, the flights a person takes between a
`board` and a `debark` carry it, and `libre` is the capacity constraint. The makespan above ignores
the $\varepsilon$-separation of PDDL 2.1 between dependent actions, and this paper proves nothing
about PDDL plans themselves. The [Instances](../instances/index.qmd) section describes the files.

[^pddl]: Planning Domain Definition Language [[FL03](#ref-FL03)], almost universally used
in AI Planning to describe domains and instances.

### Pareto fronts {#sec-fronts}

For points $y, z$ of the plane (cost, makespan), $y \preceq z$ if $y \le z$ in both coordinates.
For a set $\mathcal S$ of points, $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$ is the set of $z \in \mathcal S$
weakly dominated by no other point of $\mathcal S$, and the *Pareto front* of an instance is
$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A$ ({{< node "Definition 1.6" >}}). A list of points is *the
Pareto front of* $\mathcal S$ if its points lie in $\mathcal S$, every point of $\mathcal S$ is
weakly dominated by a listed point, and the listed points are pairwise incomparable. We look for
the front and for one plan per front point.

Every characterization of the front in this paper has two halves: a set of points that plans
attain, and a proof that every plan is weakly dominated by one of them. The following lemma turns
them into an equality of fronts.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 1.7" >}} **Dominating sets.** *(a)* If every point of $\mathcal S$ is weakly
dominated by a point of $\mathcal S'$ and every point of $\mathcal S'$ by a point of
$\mathcal S$, then $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'$; in particular when
$\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S$ and every point of $\mathcal S$ is weakly dominated by a point
of $\mathcal S'$. *(b)* A list that is the Pareto front of $\mathcal S$ lists exactly the points
of $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$.
:::

### Assumptions {#sec-assumptions}

The results of this paper use the following assumptions ({{< node "Definition 1.4" >}}), each one only
where stated. The first two are the triangular inequality and the symmetry assumption:

**Assumption**: $\forall (a, b, x),\ \mathrm{dur}(a, x) + \mathrm{dur}(x, b) \ge \mathrm{dur}(a, b)$
whenever $a \ne b$ and the three flights exist $\hfill$ (AΔ)

**Assumption** (Symmetry): $\forall i \in [1, n],\ d_i = \bar d_i$ $\hfill$ (S)

The assumption of [[QS15](#ref-QS15)], in a non-strict form, and its non-symmetric
counterpart state that flights between central cities are useless, that is, never faster than a
detour through $C_I$ or $C_G$:

**Assumption**: $\forall (i, j),\ d_{ij} \ge d_i + d_j$ $\hfill$ (A1)

**Assumption**: $\forall (i, j),\ d_{ij} \ge \min(d_i + d_j,\ \bar d_i + \bar d_j)$ $\hfill$ (A1-NS)

Finally, the symmetric results use the triangular inequality only on the triangles through the
hubs, the *hub triangles*:

**Assumption**: $\forall (i, j),\ d_j \le d_i + d_{ij}$ and $d_i \le d_{ij} + d_j$ $\hfill$ (H)

(H) is (AΔ) on the triangles $C_I \to C_i \to C_j$ against $C_I \to C_j$, and
$C_i \to C_j \to C_I$ against $C_i \to C_I$; under (S) these are also the triangles through
$C_G$. In (AΔ), the condition $a \ne b$ leaves the flights $d_{ii}$ free.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 1.5" >}} **Hub triangles.** (A1) implies (H), and (AΔ) implies (H).
:::

**Notation.** We write $s = 2t - p$, so that $s \ge p$ and $s \equiv p \pmod 2$, and
$\kappa = \lceil s/p \rceil$ ({{< node "Notation" >}}). For a multiset $Y$ of central cities,
$Y(i)$ is the multiplicity of $i$, $|Y|$ its size, $c(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} c_w$ its cost, and
$\delta(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} d_w$ and $\bar\delta(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} \bar d_w$ its durations;
with $e_i = \min(d_i, \bar d_i)$, $e(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} e_w$. Under (S), the *load* of $Y$ is
$\ell(Y) = 2\delta(Y)$. A *partition* of $X$ over the planes is a family of groups
$X_1, \dots, X_p$ with $X_1 + \dots + X_p = X$, group $X_k$ being the cities in which plane $k$
lands. $d_{\min}$, $d_{\max}$ and $c_{\min}$ are the least and largest durations and the least
cost.

### Patterns {#sec-patterns}

Cut the sequence of a plane at every visit to $C_I$ or $C_G$. Each piece, from one of them to the
next, is a *pattern* (a *segment* in the [blueprint](../proofs.qmd)). As there is no flight
between $C_I$ and $C_G$, every pattern lands in at least one central city. Depending on the
cities it starts and ends in, a pattern is of one of four types, denoted by $A$, $\bar A$, $B$ and
$\bar B$ (@fig-patterns). A pattern that lands in exactly one central city, of *multiplicity*
0, consists of two flights; we call it *simple* (a *visit* in the blueprint). We denote by $|X|$ the number of the patterns
$X \in \{A, \bar A, B, \bar B\}$ in a given plan, and by $F(\gamma)$ the flight time of a
pattern $\gamma$.

::: {#fig-patterns}

The simple patterns $A$, $\bar A$, $B$ and $\bar B$, with $I = C_I$ and $G = C_G$. In the plans
built in this paper, a pattern $A$ carries a passenger from $C_I$ to $C_G$, a pattern $\bar A$
flies back empty, a pattern $B$ leaves a passenger in $x$ and a pattern $\bar B$ takes one from
$x$ to $C_G$. Patterns of larger multiplicity have the same four types.
:::

In @fig-plan, $p_1$ performs a $B$ in $C_2$ and an $A$ in $C_3$, and $p_2$ an $A$ in $C_3$ and a
$\bar B$ in $C_2$. Only the patterns $A$ and $\bar A$ change from $C_I$ to $C_G$ or back, and a
plane goes from $C_I$ to $C_G$, so on a route of simple patterns it performs one more $A$ than
$\bar A$ ({{< node "Lemma 3.1" >}}). We deduce the following property on the number of patterns in
any feasible plan.

**Property II**: In every feasible plan,

1. at least $t$ legs leave $C_I$;
2. at least $t$ legs arrive in $C_G$;
3. on the route of each plane, the legs that leave $C_I$ and the legs that arrive in $C_G$ number
   one more than its patterns.

**Proof**: The first legs of the journeys are distinct legs from $C_I$, which proves the first
point. Apply the same reasoning to $C_G$ with the last legs of the journeys to prove the second
point. For the third point, a pattern $A$ leaves $C_I$ and arrives in $C_G$, a pattern $B$ only
leaves $C_I$, a pattern $\bar B$ only arrives in $C_G$ and a pattern $\bar A$ does neither; and a
route from $C_I$ to $C_G$ performs one more $A$ than $\bar A$, since only these two patterns change
hub. $\square$

**Corollary II** ({{< node "Lemma 3.3" >}}): A feasible plan performs at least $2t - p$ patterns:
$2t \le \sum_k h_k + p$, where $h_k$ is the number of patterns of plane $k$.

**Proof**: By Property II, $2t \le \sum_k (h_k + 1)$. $\square$

With every landing cost set to 1, {{< node "Proposition 3.6" >}} says that a feasible plan also
lands at least $2t - p$ times in central cities. With fewer planes than passengers, some planes have to come back to $C_I$, and
every return costs a landing. In @fig-plan the bound is reached: the plan lands $2t - p = 4$ times.
The [next section](#sec-front) shows that, in the symmetric case and under the hub triangles (H),
the Pareto front is always reached by such plans, and which lists of $2t - p$ cities can be flown,
and how fast.
